chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In Québec, a seller has legal obligations toward the buyer, notably the duty not to conceal defects. The seller's declaration is the tool that protects you… provided it's filled out honestly and completely.

This guide explains the legal warranty of quality, the notion of a latent defect, the role of the seller's declaration, and how to reduce your risk of a lawsuit after the sale.

Informational content, not legal advice: validate your situation with your broker and your notary. Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: The legal warranty of quality
chapters.objective: Understand what the seller commits to by default.
chapters.html:
Understand what the seller commits to by default.

In Québec, a real-estate sale generally comes with a legal warranty of quality: the seller warrants that the property is free of latent defects that would make it unfit for its use, or so diminish its usefulness that the buyer would not have bought it, or not at that price.

A latent defect is a serious flaw, not apparent on a normal examination, existing before the sale and unknown to the buyer. If such a defect appears after the sale, the buyer may have recourse against the seller.

Emilie's tip

Selling « without legal warranty, at the buyer's own risk » exists, but it changes everything for the buyer (and often the price). Never insert such a clause without understanding its consequences with your notary.

chapters.title: The seller's declaration
chapters.objective: Use this transparency tool to your advantage.
chapters.html:
Use this transparency tool to your advantage.

The seller's declaration is a form where you record what you know about the property: past infiltration, repairs, renovations (with or without a permit), known problems, presence of vermiculite, a tank, etc. Well filled out, it informs the buyer and greatly reduces the risk of a dispute.

  • Disclose what you know, honestly and completely.
  • Conceal nothing: hiding a known problem is the surest way to expose yourself to a lawsuit.
  • When in doubt about a point, it's better to mention it than to leave it out.
Emilie's tip

Transparency is your best insurance. An informed buyer who buys with full knowledge has far less recourse than a buyer who discovers a problem you knew about and didn't declare.

chapters.title: Reducing your risk of a lawsuit
chapters.objective: Protect yourself before, during and after the sale.
chapters.html:
Protect yourself before, during and after the sale.

  • Gather your proof: repair invoices, permits, expert reports.
  • Encourage the buyer to have an inspection done: a defect that's « apparent » during a normal inspection isn't a latent defect.
  • Answer questions honestly and make no false statements.
  • Keep a copy of all documents and of the signed declaration.

A complete file and total transparency are your best safeguards against a claim after the sale.

Emilie's tip

Keep all your invoices and reports, even after the sale. If a dispute arises, proving that you repaired something properly or disclosed a problem makes all the difference.

chapters.title: What to do if a problem arises
chapters.html:
React correctly to a claim.

If a buyer alleges a latent defect after the sale, they generally have to notify you (often in writing) and give you the chance to observe the problem before undertaking any work. Don't react in a panic.

  • Consult a professional quickly (notary, lawyer) to learn your rights.
  • Don't acknowledge or settle anything hastily without advice.
  • Rely on your declaration and your proof.
Emilie's tip

Faced with a claim, the worst reaction is to panic and act alone. Quick legal advice keeps you from admitting a liability you may not have.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. List all known problems, repairs and renovations.
  2. Gather invoices, permits and expert reports.

Within 30 days

  1. Fill out the seller's declaration honestly, with my broker.
  2. Encourage the buyer to have the property inspected.

Next

  1. Keep a copy of all documents after the sale.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Legal warranty of quality: protection for the buyer against latent defects.
  • Latent defect: a serious flaw, not apparent, pre-existing and unknown to the buyer.
  • Seller's declaration: a form recording what the seller knows about the property.
  • Sale without legal warranty: a clause that transfers the risk to the buyer.
  • Proof: invoices, permits and reports kept for your protection.

qcm.q: The legal warranty of quality protects against:
options: B) Serious latent defects predating the sale
qcm.explanation: A serious flaw, not apparent, pre-existing and unknown (ch. 1).

qcm.q: A latent defect is a flaw:
options: B) Not apparent on a normal examination, serious and pre-existing
B) Record what you know about the property
B) Exposes you to a lawsuit

qcm.q: A defect detected during a normal inspection:
options: B) Is not a latent defect
B) Keeping invoices, permits and reports
qcm.explanation: Proof protects you in a dispute (ch. 3).

qcm.q: If the buyer alleges a defect, they generally have to:
options: B) Notify you and let you observe it
qcm.explanation: Notice and a chance to observe are required (ch. 4).

qcm.q: Faced with a claim, you should:
qcm.explanation: Legal advice keeps you from admitting undue liability (ch. 4).
